The effect of missed or delayed PK samples around Tmax on NCA PK parameters

Jerry Hu

2026-05-30

1 Summary

Background. Real blood-sampling schedules deviate from plan. A sample near the peak can be missed, or drawn not at its planned time. The objective is to quantify how much a single missed or delayed sample around Tmax biases the key NCA exposure parameters (Cmax, AUC0-t, AUC0-inf) relative to an intact schedule.

Methods. Simulation, NCA, tables and figures, and the statistical analysis were all conducted in R. Concentration–time data were simulated from three one-compartment oral pharmacokinetic models with differing absorption and elimination rates, from 0 to 24 h after a single oral dose (20 subjects per model). The time of peak was held fixed, so the three profiles differ only in peak shape, from sharp to flat. Four sampling schedules were applied to the same subjects: a near-continuous Dense grid, an Intact 13-sample schedule, an Omission arm with the near-peak sample dropped, and a Delay arm with that sample drawn 10 minutes late. NCA derived Cmax, AUC0-t and AUC0-inf from each schedule. Each perturbed arm was then compared with the intact schedule in the same subjects, as a paired geometric mean ratio with a 90% confidence interval on the log scale.

Results. A missed near-peak sample lowered Cmax by 2.6-7.7% across shapes, while it moved AUC0-t and AUC0-inf by under 2%. A delayed sample, analysed at its recorded time, changed every parameter by roughly 1–3% or less. Across both perturbations the largest change was in Cmax; a single missed or delayed near-peak sample moved NCA exposure only slightly.

2 Background

Blood-sampling schedules in clinical pharmacokinetics are finite and planned in advance. The non-compartmental (NCA) parameters they yield — Cmax, Tmax, and the areas under the curve (AUC) — feed exposure and labelling decisions. Unplanned deviations may disturb those schedules: a sample is missed, and a sample is drawn late. The peak region is where this should matter most, because that is where the concentration is changing fastest and where Cmax and Tmax are defined.

Objective. Quantify how much a single missed or delayed sample around Tmax biases the key NCA exposure parameters (Cmax, AUC0-t, AUC0-inf) relative to an intact schedule.

3 Methods

3.1 Simulation

3.1.1 Data origin

The data were simulated with the R package mrgsolve (seed 2.0260525^{7}). The structural model is one compartment with first-order oral absorption: a dosing compartment (GUT) feeds a central compartment (CENT), parameterised by absorption rate ka, clearance CL, and volume V. The model is shown below as both a diagram and equations.

One-compartment model with first-order oral absorption. Dose enters the GUT compartment, is absorbed into CENT at rate ka, and is cleared from CENT at rate CL/V.

\[ \frac{dA_{\mathrm{GUT}}}{dt} = -k_a\,A_{\mathrm{GUT}}, \qquad \frac{dA_{\mathrm{CENT}}}{dt} = k_a\,A_{\mathrm{GUT}} - \frac{CL}{V}\,A_{\mathrm{CENT}}, \qquad C = \frac{A_{\mathrm{CENT}}}{V}. \]

where \(A_{\mathrm{GUT}}\) is the amount of drug in the absorption (gut) compartment, \(A_{\mathrm{CENT}}\) the amount in the central compartment, \(k_a\) the first-order absorption rate constant, \(CL\) the clearance, \(V\) the central volume of distribution, and \(C\) the plasma concentration (\(C = A_{\mathrm{CENT}}/V\)).

The model is defined in mrgsolve. The $OMEGA and $SIGMA blocks carry the between-subject and residual variability described below:

# --- truth model ----------------------------------------------------
# OMEGA = log(1 + CV^2) for 30% log-normal CV ≈ 0.0862 (variance scale).
# SIGMA = (0.10)^2 = 0.01 for 10% proportional RUV (variance scale).
.model_code <- '
$PARAM
TVKA = 5.2, TVCL = 25, TVV = 50

$CMT GUT CENT

$OMEGA @labels ETA_KA ETA_CL ETA_V
0.0862 0.0862 0.0862

$SIGMA @labels PROP
0.01

$PK
double KA = TVKA * exp(ETA_KA);
double CL = TVCL * exp(ETA_CL);
double V  = TVV  * exp(ETA_V);

$ODE
dxdt_GUT  = -KA * GUT;
dxdt_CENT =  KA * GUT - (CL/V) * CENT;

$ERROR
double IPRED = CENT / V;
double DV = IPRED * (1 + PROP);

$CAPTURE IPRED DV KA CL V
'

mod <- mrgsolve::mcode("oral_1cmt_truth", .model_code, quiet = TRUE)

Between-subject variability is log-normal on ka, CL and V (30% coefficient of variation each). Residual error is proportional (10%). Three scenarios share V = 50 L and hold the time of peak at about 0.5 h, differing only in how fast the drug is eliminated relative to how fast it is absorbed:

The three profile shapes. Tmax is held near 0.5 h across all three, so the perturbed sample lands in the same place each time.
Scenario ka (1/h) CL (L/h) V (L) t1/2 (h) Shape
Sharp 9.1 5 50 6.93 Narrow peak, slow decay (post-Tmax)
Medium 5.2 25 50 1.39 Moderate peak and decay
Broad 3.3 55 50 0.63 Wide peak, fast decay

Each scenario has 20 subjects. The three scenarios share the design constants and are simulated over a 1-min grid (later thinned to each sampling schedule):

# V = 50 L throughout; CL chosen so kel = CL/V matches each scenario.
# All three give Tmax in [0.495, 0.505] h via ln(ka/kel)/(ka-kel).
scenario_params <- list(
  sharp  = list(TVKA = 9.1, TVCL = 0.1 * 50, TVV = 50),
  medium = list(TVKA = 5.2, TVCL = 0.5 * 50, TVV = 50),
  broad  = list(TVKA = 3.3, TVCL = 1.1 * 50, TVV = 50)
)

# --- design constants -----------------------------------------------
N_SUBJ        <- 20
DOSE_MG       <- 100
NOMINAL_TIMES <- c(0, 0.25, 0.5, 0.75, 1, 1.5, 2, 3, 4, 6, 8, 12, 24)
DELAY_TIME    <- 0.5 + 10/60                       # 10-min delay → 0.6667 h
DENSE_GRID    <- seq(0, 24, by = 1/60)             # 1-min resolution

# --- simulate -------------------------------------------------------
simulate_scenario <- function(scenario_name, pars) {
  mod_s <- param(mod, pars)
  events <- expand.ev(ID = seq_len(N_SUBJ), amt = DOSE_MG, cmt = 1)
  all_times <- sort(unique(c(DENSE_GRID, NOMINAL_TIMES, DELAY_TIME)))

  sim <- mod_s |>
    data_set(events) |>
    mrgsim(end = 24, add = all_times, obsonly = TRUE) |>
    as.data.frame()

  # ODE solver can return tiny negatives at late times when true concentration
  # is ~machine epsilon (broad scenario, t > ~10 h). Clip at 0.
  sim$IPRED <- pmax(sim$IPRED, 0)
  sim$DV    <- pmax(sim$DV,    0)
  sim$SCENARIO <- scenario_name
  sim
}

3.1.2 Sampling schedule

Four sampling schedules are applied to the same per-subject time-courses, so each subject acts as its own control across arms:

Four sampling arms. The Dense arm is re-simulated from the same model, seed, and per-subject random effects, so all comparisons are within-subject.
Arm # samples (0-24 h) Time grid (h) Role
Dense 1441 0 to 24 every 1/60 h (1-min resolution) Calibration reference (near-continuous)
Intact 13 0, 0.25, 0.5, 0.75, 1, 1.5, 2, 3, 4, 6, 8, 12, 24 Reference: practical schedule
Omission 12 Intact grid with the 0.5 h sample dropped Missed near-Tmax sample
Delay 13 Intact grid but the 0.5 h slot is drawn at 0.667 h (+10 min) Delayed near-Tmax sample

The Intact 13-sample schedule is the reference. The Omission and Delay arms each perturb the single 0.5 h near-peak slot. The Dense per-minute arm is a calibration reference, showing how a practical schedule compares with near-continuous sampling.

The three practical arms are built from the same simulated time-courses by selecting times: Omission drops the 0.5 h slot, and Delay replaces it with the 0.667 h draw:

# --- arms -----------------------------------------------------------
baseline <- scenarios_sim |>
  filter(in_set(time, NOMINAL_TIMES)) |>
  transmute(SCENARIO, ID, ARM = "baseline",
            TIME_NOMINAL = round(time, 6),
            TIME_ACTUAL  = round(time, 6),
            CONC = DV)

omission <- baseline |>
  filter(!near(TIME_NOMINAL, 0.5)) |>
  mutate(ARM = "omission")

delayed_sample <- scenarios_sim |>
  filter(in_set(time, DELAY_TIME)) |>
  transmute(SCENARIO, ID, ARM = "delay",
            TIME_NOMINAL = 0.5,
            TIME_ACTUAL  = round(time, 6),
            CONC = DV)

delay <- bind_rows(
  baseline |> filter(!near(TIME_NOMINAL, 0.5)) |> mutate(ARM = "delay"),
  delayed_sample
) |> arrange(SCENARIO, ID, TIME_ACTUAL)

obs <- bind_rows(baseline, omission, delay)

3.2 NCA

NCA is performed with the R package PKNCA, over the 0–last and 0–inf intervals, using the linear-up / log-down trapezoidal rule for the AUC. The reported parameters are Cmax, AUC0-t and AUC0-inf (primary) and Tmax (secondary). Dose is treated as known and fixed, so only dose-independent parameters are reported. The pipeline is standardised across all arms, so any difference between arms reflects the sampling perturbation rather than analyst choices. Each arm is run through the same PKNCA call, at the actual sample times:

# PKNCA computes lambda.z internally to extrapolate aucinf.obs; we request it so
# the dependency is explicit, but it is not carried into the wide frame.
NCA_INTERVAL <- data.frame(
  start      = 0,
  end        = Inf,
  cmax       = TRUE,
  tmax       = TRUE,
  auclast    = TRUE,
  aucinf.obs = TRUE,
  lambda.z   = TRUE
)

# Parameters carried into the wide results frame (SAP-reported only).
NCA_PARAMS_WIDE <- c("cmax", "tmax", "auclast", "aucinf.obs")

#' Run NCA on a single arm across all (SCENARIO, ID), at the actual sample times.
#'
#' @param obs       Long observation data (SCENARIO, ID, ARM, TIME_*, CONC).
#' @param arm       Arm to subset ("baseline", "omission", "delay").
#' @param run_label Label tagged onto the output (e.g. "INTACT").
#' @return Long PKNCA result with RUN_LABEL attached.
run_nca_slice <- function(obs, arm, run_label) {
  stopifnot(arm %in% unique(obs$ARM))

  sub <- obs %>%
    filter(ARM == arm) %>%
    transmute(SCENARIO, ID, TIME = TIME_ACTUAL, CONC) %>%
    arrange(SCENARIO, ID, TIME)

  conc_obj <- PKNCAconc(sub, CONC ~ TIME | SCENARIO + ID)
  dose_df <- sub %>% distinct(SCENARIO, ID) %>% mutate(TIME = 0, DOSE = 1)
  dose_obj <- PKNCAdose(dose_df, DOSE ~ TIME | SCENARIO + ID)

  pk_res <- pk.nca(PKNCAdata(conc_obj, dose_obj, intervals = NCA_INTERVAL))
  out <- as.data.frame(pk_res$result)
  out$RUN_LABEL <- run_label
  out
}

3.3 Statistical analysis

All comparisons are paired by subject, and the analysis was pre-specified before results.

For each of the three ratio parameters (Cmax, AUC0-t, AUC0-inf), the estimand is the per-subject log-ratio of the perturbed schedule to the intact schedule, summarised as the geometric mean ratio, GMR = exp(mean of the per-subject log-ratios). The log transform is a pre-specified preliminary step. Each GMR is reported with a 90% confidence interval from the paired t-distribution on the log scale; 100% denotes no effect.

Tmax is summarised descriptively, as the median within-subject shift in hours, because it is a time on a discrete grid.

The estimator takes the per-subject log-ratios, averages them, and back-transforms the mean and its paired-t interval to the ratio scale:

#' GMR + 90% CI for the ratio parameters (paired log-scale estimator).
#' @return per (SCENARIO, parameter, contrast): n, gmr, ci_lo, ci_hi.
gmr_summary <- function(pairs) {
  pairs %>%
    filter(parameter %in% PARAMS_RATIO,
           is.finite(theta_test), is.finite(theta_ref),
           theta_test > 0, theta_ref > 0) %>%
    group_by(SCENARIO, parameter, contrast) %>%
    summarise(
      n            = n(),
      mean_logdiff = mean(log(theta_test) - log(theta_ref)),
      sd_logdiff   = sd(log(theta_test) - log(theta_ref)),
      .groups = "drop"
    ) %>%
    mutate(
      se        = sd_logdiff / sqrt(n),
      tcrit     = qt(0.95, n - 1),          # 90% CI -> 0.95 one-sided quantile
      gmr       = exp(mean_logdiff),
      ci_lo     = exp(mean_logdiff - tcrit * se),
      ci_hi     = exp(mean_logdiff + tcrit * se)
    ) %>%
    select(scenario = SCENARIO, parameter, contrast,
           n, gmr, ci_lo, ci_hi)
}

4.1 Simulation

The Dense arm traces the underlying concentration-time signal at high resolution. Across the three shapes the time of peak is held near 0.5 h, so each profile differs only in how sharply it rises and falls.

Zooming on the peak over the first 4 h shows how the practical arms sample it. The Omission and Delay arms each perturb the single 0.5 h near-peak slot, so any divergence between arms is most visible there.

4.3 Statistical analysis

The forest plot and table report each geometric mean ratio with its 90% CI, by parameter and scenario. A missed near-peak sample lowered Cmax by 2.6-7.7% across the three shapes (geometric mean ratio 92.32%-97.38%) and moved AUC0-t and AUC0-inf by under 2%. A delayed sample, analysed at its recorded time, changed Cmax by -1.6-4.2% (geometric mean ratio 95.79%-101.59%) and both AUCs by about 1% or less.

These ratios span several parameters and scenarios. They are read as ranges describing magnitude, not as multiplicity-controlled tests.

The calibration contrast puts the perturbations in context: the intact 13-sample schedule itself recovers Cmax only to 86.41%-88.07% of the per-minute Dense reference. That gap — larger than either perturbation — is a property of discrete sampling. A 13-point grid rarely lands on the true peak, and the Dense grid samples the proportional residual error far more often, inflating its Cmax.

4.4 Results Summary

The objective was to quantify how much a single missed or delayed sample around Tmax biases the key NCA exposure parameters (Cmax, AUC0-t, AUC0-inf) relative to an intact schedule. Across the three profile shapes:

Effect on Cmax.

  • Omission vs Intact: Cmax was 92.32%-97.38% of intact (lower by 2.6-7.7%) — the largest effect of either perturbation, because dropping the near-peak sample widens the gap between the sampled maximum and the true peak.
  • Delay vs Intact: Cmax was 95.79%-101.59% of intact (within -1.6-4.2%); the sample drawn 10 min late still lands near the peak.

Effect on AUC (AUC0-t and AUC0-inf).

  • Both perturbations moved AUC0-t and AUC0-inf by under 2% relative to intact; one near-peak point is a small part of the exposure integral.

Effect on Tmax.

  • Omission moved the recorded median Tmax to the next scheduled time, since the 0.5 h sample is absent; Delay recorded the actual +10 min draw time. The largest median Tmax shift across perturbations was 10 min.

5 Discussion

We simulated single-dose concentration–time data from three one-compartment oral PK models spanning fast to slow elimination, applied four sampling schedules to the same subjects, derived the NCA parameters from each, and compared each perturbed schedule with the intact schedule as a paired geometric mean ratio with a 90% confidence interval. The findings, and the caveat specific to each, are:

  • Cmax. A missed near-peak sample produced the largest change, lowering Cmax by 2.6-7.7%; a sample drawn 10 min late changed it by -1.6-4.2%. These ratios are relative to the intact practical schedule, not to the true peak, and they assume the deviation falls on the near-Tmax sample; a deviation elsewhere on the curve would affect Cmax less.
  • AUC. AUC0-t and AUC0-inf moved by under 2% under either perturbation, because a single near-peak point is a small fraction of the integral. This would not hold for deviations during the absorption phase or for several missing points.
  • Tmax. Omission shifts the recorded Tmax to the next scheduled time and Delay records the later draw time, so Tmax tracks the sampling times directly. Tmax is a discrete-grid maximum and is sensitive to residual noise: even the near-continuous Dense arm has an upward-biased median Tmax (0.65 h for the slow-decay Sharp scenario, versus the 0.5 h design value), because the maximum of noisy concentrations on a flat, slowly-declining peak tends to fall on a later timepoint. Observed Tmax should therefore be read as approximate.
  • The sampling grid is the larger source of Cmax bias. The intact 13-sample schedule recovers Cmax only to 86.41%-88.07% of the per-minute Dense reference — a wider gap than either perturbation, and structural to discrete sampling. The Dense Cmax is itself inflated, because high-resolution sampling of the 10% proportional residual error raises the observed maximum.

Other limitations.

  • A single delay magnitude (+10 min on the 0.5 h slot), a single missed slot, and 20 subjects per scenario isolate the structural effect but bound generalisation. Larger delays, multiple deviations, and deviations at later timepoints would give different numbers.
  • The reference is the intact practical schedule, not model truth, so the Cmax comparisons are “perturbed vs intact practical schedule”, not “vs the true peak”.

Data and code availability. The pipeline is staged and reproducible from its entry scripts, run in order: 01-simulate/simulate.R (writes the simulated observations), 02-analyze/analyze.R (NCA and the paired geometric mean ratios), 03-tlf/build_tlf.R (the results bundle this report reads), and 04-report/report.Rmd (this document). The Dense per-minute reference is regenerated from the model and seed (2.0260525^{7}).
